games.title: MS Excel — HIT100 Course: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 1 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which MS Excel function should a medical student use to calculate the mean systolic blood pressure from a dataset of 30 patients stored in cells A1 to A30?
questions.explanation: The AVERAGE function calculates the arithmetic mean of a specified range of numeric values.

questions.q: A researcher wishes to calculate Body Mass Index (BMI) in Excel where patient weight (in kg) is in cell B2 and height (in meters) is in cell C2. What is the correct formula syntax?
questions.explanation: BMI is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared, which is represented in Excel as =B2/(C2^2).

questions.q: Which MS Excel feature allows a clinician to automatically highlight all patient blood glucose values that exceed 11.1 mmol/L in red?
questions.explanation: Conditional Formatting changes the visual appearance of cells dynamically based on specified rules or cell values.

questions.q: When copying a formula down a column of drug dosage calculations, which symbol is used to create an absolute cell reference to prevent a specific constant cell from changing?
questions.explanation: The dollar sign ($) is used in Excel formulas to fix a column or row reference as absolute.

questions.q: Which function correctly counts the total number of patients diagnosed with "Hypertension" in a dataset range E2 to E100?
questions.explanation: The COUNTIF function counts the number of cells within a specified range that meet a single specified criterion.

questions.q: What Excel feature allows an epidemiologist to quickly summarize, aggregate, and cross-tabulate thousands of patient health records by hospital ward and diagnosis?
questions.explanation: PivotTables are interactive analytical tools used to quickly summarize and analyze large datasets.

questions.q: To prevent data entry errors in a electronic ward register by restricting heart rate inputs strictly to numbers between 30 and 220 bpm, which Excel tool should be configured?
questions.explanation: Data Validation sets explicit restriction rules on the type and range of data users can enter into a given cell.

questions.q: Which formula correctly returns the youngest age from a list of pediatric patient ages entered in cells D2 through D45?
questions.explanation: The MIN function evaluates a numerical range and returns the smallest value within that set.

questions.q: A medical student needs to search for a patient's diagnosis in column B by looking up their unique Medical Record Number (MRN) in column A. Which function is designed for this task?
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP searches vertically down the first column of a range for a key value and returns data from the same row in a specified column.

questions.q: A public health student wants to graph continuous daily COVID-19 hospital admission trends over a 6-month period. Which chart type is best suited for this purpose?
questions.explanation: Line charts are designed to show continuous trends and tracking of quantitative data over continuous intervals of time.

games.title: Chest Trauma and Chest Drain (Underwater Seal Drainage): quick quiz
games.topic: Chest Trauma and Chest Drain (Underwater Seal Drainage)
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: What is the immediate emergency intervention for a patient presenting with clinical signs of a tension pneumothorax before a chest drain can be inserted?
options: Needle thoracocentesis in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line or 4th/5th intercostal space anterior axillary line
Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask as the sole initial measure
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression via needle thoracocentesis before confirmatory imaging or definitive chest drain placement.

questions.q: Which of the following ongoing hourly blood outputs from a chest drain is an indication for emergency exploratory thoracotomy following traumatic hemothorax?
questions.explanation: An initial drain output greater than 1500 mL or persistent bleeding of more than 200 mL/hour for 2 to 4 hours indicates major vascular injury requiring emergency thoracotomy.

questions.q: Which anatomical landmark defines the anterior boundary of the 'triangle of safety' used for safe chest drain insertion?
options: Anterior border of the latissimus dorsi
Lateral border of the pectoralis major
questions.explanation: The triangle of safety is bounded anteriorly by the lateral border of the pectoralis major, posteriorly by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, and inferiorly by the 5th intercostal space.

questions.q: While monitoring a patient with an underwater seal chest drain, persistent continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber throughout the respiratory cycle indicates which of the following?
options: An ongoing air leak from the lung parenchymal defect or system
questions.explanation: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal bottle during both inspiration and expiration signifies a active, persistent air leak from the respiratory tract or a breach in the external tubing system.

questions.q: To prevent damage to the intercostal neurovascular bundle during tube thoracostomy, the chest drain must be inserted in which location relative to the ribs?
options: Directly under the inferior border of the rib above
Just over the superior border of the rib below
Directly in the middle of the intercostal space
Traversing directly through the rib cartilage
questions.explanation: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run along the subcostal groove at the lower border of each rib, so instruments and tubes must be passed just superior to the lower rib.

questions.q: A patient presents with an open pneumothorax ('sucking chest wound') following a penetrating injury. What is the correct initial pre-hospital dressing application?
options: Fully occlusive dressing taped securely on all four sides
Three-sided occlusive dressing acting as a one-way flutter valve
Gauze packing directly inside the chest wound cavity
Tension dressing applied tightly around the entire chest circumference
questions.explanation: A three-sided occlusive dressing permits trapped air to escape from the pleural space during expiration while preventing air entry during inspiration, reducing the risk of developing a tension pneumothorax.

questions.q: In a patient with a flail chest, what is the primary underlying pathological contributor to severe hypoxemia?
options: Paradoxical inward movement of the chest wall alone
questions.explanation: While paradoxical chest movement causes pain and mechanical inefficiency, underlying pulmonary contusion with parenchymal hemorrhage and edema is the main cause of hypoxemia in flail chest.

questions.q: During spontaneous breathing in a patient with a chest drain, what movement of the fluid column in the underwater seal tube is expected during inspiration?
options: The fluid column remains completely stationary
The fluid column empties completely into the collection chamber
questions.explanation: In a spontaneously breathing patient, negative intrapleural pressure generated during inspiration draws the fluid column upward in the underwater seal tubing ('tidalling').

questions.q: A hemodynamically stable blunt chest trauma patient has a chest X-ray showing a widened mediastinum and loss of the aortic knob contour. What is the gold-standard diagnostic imaging modality to confirm suspected traumatic aortic disruption?
options: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
Contrast-enhanced Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) of the chest
Repeat plain chest radiograph in 4 hours
questions.explanation: CTA of the chest is the gold standard imaging investigation for diagnosing traumatic aortic disruption in a hemodynamically stable patient.

questions.q: Which of the following findings is a key requirement before safely removing a chest drain inserted for a pneumothorax?
options: Presence of active tidalling in the drain tubing
Demonstration of continuous bubbling on coughing
Complete lung re-expansion on chest X-ray with no air leak for at least 24 hours
questions.explanation: A chest drain for pneumothorax can be safely removed when clinical and chest X-ray evidence confirms complete lung re-expansion, fluid output is minimal, and there has been no air leak for at least 24 hours.

games.title: Sickle cell anemia: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male with known sickle cell anemia (HbSS) presents to the emergency department with severe, deep aching pain in both thighs and chest for 6 hours. He is afebrile, his oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and his hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL (baseline 7.8 g/dL). What is the most appropriate initial management step?
options: Intravenous hydration and aggressive opioid analgesia
Immediate red blood cell exchange transfusion
questions.explanation: Initial management of an uncomplicated acute vaso-occlusive crisis centers on prompt analgesia and adequate intravenous or oral hydration.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female with sickle cell disease admitted for a vaso-occlusive crisis develops new-onset fever (38.8°C), cough, tachypnea, and chest pain. Her oxygen saturation drops to 89% on room air, and a chest radiograph demonstrates a new consolidation in the right lower lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is defined in sickle cell patients by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography combined with fever, respiratory distress, or hypoxia.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male with sickle cell anemia presents with severe fatigue and pallor over the past two days. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin of 3.2 g/dL (baseline 8.0 g/dL) and a reticulocyte count of 0.1%. What is the most likely etiology for this patient's acute decompensation?
questions.explanation: A profound drop in hemoglobin accompanied by reticulocytopenia in a patient with sickle cell disease is characteristic of an aplastic crisis, most commonly caused by Parvovirus B19.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with a painful, persistent erection lasting for more than 4 hours. Conservative measures, including hydration and analgesia, have failed to achieve detumescence. What is the next best step in management?
options: Aspiration of blood from the corpus cavernosum followed by intracavernosal alpha-agonist injection
Immediate simple red blood cell transfusion
Application of warm compresses and outpatient urology follow-up
questions.explanation: Ischemic priapism lasting longer than 4 hours is a medical emergency requiring penile aspiration and intracavernosal injection of an alpha-adrenergic agonist like phenylephrine.

questions.q: A 21-year-old female with sickle cell disease is started on hydroxyurea to reduce the frequency of her vaso-occlusive crises. Follow-up lab work demonstrates an increased fetal hemoglobin (HbF) percentage. Which mechanism of action accounts for the primary therapeutic effect of this medication?
options: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase to increase fetal hemoglobin synthesis
Direct binding and chemical inhibition of hemoglobin S polymerization
Selective antagonism of P-selectin on endothelial cells
Replenishment of intracellular L-glutamine levels in erythrocytes
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, which stimulates fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production and reduces HbS polymerization and vaso-occlusion.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male with HbSS disease presents with sudden-onset right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia lasting 2 hours. A non-contrast head CT rules out hemorrhage, and MRI confirms an acute ischemic stroke. What is the most appropriate acute definitive management to prevent further neurological injury?
options: Emergency exchange transfusion to lower HbS to less than 30%
High-dose dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel
Immediate lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
questions.explanation: Acute ischemic stroke in patients with sickle cell anemia is primarily managed with urgent exchange transfusion to reduce HbS concentrations below 30% without raising hyperviscosity.

questions.q: A 23-year-old male with sickle cell anemia presents with left thigh pain, swelling, and fever. Magnetic resonance imaging confirms osteomyelitis of the femur, and blood cultures grow gram-negative bacilli. Which organism is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in this patient population?
questions.explanation: Due to functional asplenia and bone microinfarctions, patients with sickle cell disease are uniquely predisposed to osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella species alongside Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.q: A 26-year-old female with sickle cell disease presents with recurrent right upper quadrant abdominal pain triggered by fatty meals. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing within the gallbladder. What is the main structural component of these gallstones?
questions.explanation: Chronic intravascular hemolysis in sickle cell disease leads to increased bilirubin turnover and precipitation of calcium bilirubinate (pigment) gallstones.

games.title: Pneumothorax: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 22-year-old tall, thin male presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath while resting. On physical examination, he has absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right hemithorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Young, tall, thin males are at highest risk for primary spontaneous pneumothorax due to the rupture of apical blebs.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history and severe emphysema presents with acute worsening of dyspnea and left-sided chest pain. His trachea is midline, blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and breath sounds are significantly reduced on the left. A chest radiograph demonstrates a visceral pleural line without a shift of the mediastinum. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces in older patients with underlying lung disease generally warrant active intervention with chest tube insertion rather than observation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male is brought to the trauma bay following a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is in severe respiratory distress with absent breath sounds on the right, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation to the left. What is the immediate life-saving intervention?
options: Urgent computed tomography of the chest
questions.explanation: This patient presents with classic signs of a tension pneumothorax requiring immediate needle decompression before confirmatory imaging or chest tube placement.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease undergoes a routine follow-up chest radiograph, which incidentally reveals a small, asymptomatic right-sided pneumothorax occupying less than 15% of the hemithorax. Her vital signs are completely normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Small, stable primary or secondary pneumothoraces can often be managed conservatively with supplemental oxygen and observation in a monitored setting.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with acute right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began on the second day of her menses. She has had similar milder episodes in the past that resolved spontaneously. What is the most likely underlying etiology of her pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Catamenial pneumothorax is linked to thoracic endometriosis and typically occurs synchronously with menstruation in women of reproductive age.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male with HIV and a history of recurrent pneumothoraces undergoes a chest CT scan, which reveals multiple thin-walled cystic air spaces bilaterally throughout all lung fields. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in immunocompromised patients frequently causes necrotizing lung lesions that can lead to pneumothorax.

questions.q: An otherwise healthy 19-year-old college student undergoes a chest radiograph for a large primary spontaneous pneumothorax that fails to resolve after 48 hours of chest tube drainage with ongoing air leak. What is the next best management step?
questions.explanation: Persistent air leak after 48 to 72 hours or recurrent pneumothorax is an indication for surgical intervention such as VATS with blebectomy and pleurodesis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male is being mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit for acute respiratory distress syndrome. He suddenly develops high peak airway pressures, decreased oxygen saturation, and absent breath sounds on the left side. What is the most urgent diagnostic modality or intervention?
options: Immediate needle decompression or chest tube placement
questions.explanation: Patients receiving positive pressure ventilation who develop a tension pneumothorax require immediate decompression, as clinical instability precludes waiting for imaging.

games.title: Acne Vulgaris & Rosacea: Pathology, Symptoms, & Treatment: drug duel
games.topic: Acne Vulgaris & Rosacea: Pathology, Symptoms, & Treatment
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 21-year-old woman with severe nodulocystic acne is started on oral isotretinoin. Which laboratory monitoring parameter is essential due to a common metabolic adverse effect of this medication?
questions.explanation: Oral isotretinoin frequently causes hypertriglyceridemia and elevated liver enzymes, necessitating baseline and periodic monitoring of serum lipids and liver function.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with persistent facial erythema secondary to erythematotelangiectatic rosacea. Which topical drug acts as a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist to temporarily reduce facial redness via cutaneous vasoconstriction?
questions.explanation: Topical brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces persistent facial erythema in rosacea through direct cutaneous vasoconstriction.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action best describes how topical benzoyl peroxide treats acne vulgaris?
options: Generation of reactive oxygen species that kill Cutibacterium acnes
Selective inhibition of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit
questions.explanation: Benzoyl peroxide releases free radicals that decompose bacterial proteins and kill Cutibacterium acnes while also providing mild keratolytic activity.

questions.q: A 19-year-old man taking oral doxycycline for moderate acne vulgaris presents with severe headache, papilledema, and visual changes. Co-administration of which acne medication significantly increases the risk of this condition?
questions.explanation: Concomitant administration of oral tetracyclines such as doxycycline and oral isotretinoin significantly increases the risk of developing pseudotumor cerebri.

questions.q: Topical tretinoin is a mainstay of acne vulgaris therapy. What is its primary therapeutic mechanism of action in treating comedonal acne?
options: Direct bactericidal activity against Cutibacterium acnes
Normalisation of follicular keratinisation and desquamation
Systemic suppression of serum testosterone levels
questions.explanation: Topical retinoids bind retinoic acid receptors to normalize follicular desquamation, preventing microcomedone formation and clearing existing comedones.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with papulopustular rosacea and is prescribed topical metronidazole. What is the primary mechanism by which metronidazole reduces rosacea lesions?
options: Reduction of inflammatory reactive oxygen species
Direct keratolytic breakdown of closed comedones
questions.explanation: Topical metronidazole treats papulopustular rosacea predominantly through anti-inflammatory effects, including the reduction of neutrophil-generated reactive oxygen species.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with adult-onset facial and jawline acne vulgaris is prescribed oral spironolactone. Which adverse effect should be routinely monitored during therapy?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone acts as an aldosterone antagonist with anti-androgenic effects, placing patients at risk for hyperkalemia and menstrual irregularities.

questions.q: Which topical agent used in acne vulgaris and rosacea acts by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis and competitively inhibiting tyrosinase, making it helpful for co-existing post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation?
questions.explanation: Azelaic acid provides antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and comedolytic effects, while its inhibition of tyrosinase helps improve post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

games.title: Cough: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of dextromethorphan when used for cough suppression?
options: Peripheral antagonism of peripheral sensory cough receptors in the respiratory tract
Central depression of the medullary cough center via NMDA receptor antagonism
Inhibition of histamine H1 receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle
Direct relaxation of airway smooth muscle through phosphodiesterase inhibition
questions.explanation: Dextromethorphan acts centrally by elevating the threshold of the medullary cough center through NMDA receptor antagonism.

questions.q: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presents with a persistent, dry, irritating cough two weeks after starting a new cardiovascular medication. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril frequently cause a dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin and substance P.

questions.q: What is the primary pharmacological class of benzonatate, a non-narcotic oral antitussive agent?
questions.explanation: Benzonatate acts as a peripheral local anesthetic, anesthetizing the stretch receptors in the respiratory passages, lungs, and pleura.

questions.q: Which characteristic side effect is classically associated with the use of codeine as an antitussive agent?
questions.explanation: Codeine is an opioid that commonly causes constipation due to decreased gastrointestinal motility resulting from mu-opioid receptor activation.

questions.q: Which of the following medications functions primarily as a mucolytic agent by splitting disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins?
questions.explanation: Acetylcysteine acts as a mucolytic by opening disulfide bonds in mucus via its free sulfhydryl group, thereby lowering mucus viscosity.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of guaifenesin, a commonly used expectorant?
options: Suppression of the cough reflex in the medulla
Irritation of gastric vagal receptors leading to increased respiratory tract secretions
Direct lysis of DNA strands in purulent respiratory secretions
questions.explanation: Guaifenesin is thought to act by irritating gastric vagal receptors, which reflexively stimulate serous secretions in the respiratory tract to increase the volume and decrease the viscosity of sputum.

questions.q: A patient with chronic bronchitis is prescribed erdosteine. To which pharmacological class does this drug belong?
questions.explanation: Erdosteine is a mucolytic agent that contains blocked sulfhydryl groups, which are released after hepatic metabolism to fluidify mucus and reduce bacterial adhesion.

questions.q: Which of the following antitussive agents is a synthetic opioid derivative that lacks analgesic properties and has a low addictive profile at therapeutic doses?
questions.explanation: Dextromethorphan is the d-isomer of the morphine analogue levorphanol and acts as an antitussive without significant opioid analgesia or dependence at standard doses.
